say: You give it a change in some quantity and the time it took. It finds the **rate**: how much the quantity changes in each unit of time.
The key idea: rate is change divided by time. For a journey in parts, add up the total change and the total time first, then divide once.

how.higher: Higher level uses it as a step inside bigger questions: in 2023 Paper 1 Q7(f) it is time = distance ÷ speed for a 10 km journey (5 marks), and in 2017 Paper 2 Q2(d)(i) it compares two journey times (5 marks).
how.ordinary: Ordinary level asks for it on Paper 1 as a part of its own, usually worth 10 marks: speed = distance ÷ time read from a graph (2024 Q8), or the time for a journey at a given speed (2023 Q5, 2021 Q10).

example.question: A cyclist rides $18$ km in $45$ minutes, then $12$ km in $15$ minutes. Find her average speed for the whole journey, in km/h.

steps.title: Change minutes to hours
steps.say: Speed in km/h needs the time in **hours**. Divide each number of minutes by $60$.

steps.title: Add the totals
steps.say: Do not average the two speeds. Add up the whole distance and the whole time.

steps.title: Divide distance by time
steps.say: Average speed is the total distance divided by the total time.

lines.text: The two speeds were $24$ and $48$ km/h. The average is not $36$, because she spent longer at the slower speed.

higher.tip: Write the formula you are using, time = distance ÷ speed, before you substitute. Marks are given for it.
Give the unit the question asks for. An answer in the wrong unit loses a mark.
If the question asks for minutes, convert. An answer left in hours only reaches high partial credit.

ordinary.tip: Read off both values, distance and time, then substitute into speed = distance ÷ time. Marks are given for each step.
When a time is asked for in hours, leave it as a fraction such as $\frac{2}{3}$. Writing 40 minutes or $0.67$ costs a mark.
Do not round part way through. Rounding early so that it changes the answer is penalised.
An answer without units can still earn full marks, but write the units anyway.

say: You give it a future sum $F$, a yearly rate $i$ and a time $t$. It finds the amount $P$ you would have to invest **today** to reach $F$.
The key idea: compound interest multiplies by $(1+i)^t$, so going backwards means dividing by it.

how.higher: Higher level asks for it on Paper 1: as a 10-mark part of its own (2023 Q8(b), with a definition in words as well), and as the first step inside a loan question (2024 Q7(b)).

example.question: How much should be invested today at $3.5\%$ per annum compound interest to have €8000 in $4$ years? Give your answer to the nearest cent.

steps.title: Start from compound interest
steps.say: After $t$ years, $P$ grows to $F = P(1+i)^t$. The present value goes the other way, so divide to find $P$.

steps.title: Write down the values
steps.say: Turn the rate into a decimal: $3.5\% = 0.035$.

steps.title: Substitute
steps.say: Put the numbers into the formula for $\hl{1}{P}$.

steps.title: Work it out
steps.say: Use the calculator, and round to the nearest cent at the end.

higher.tip: Be ready to say what present value means: the amount invested today that grows to the future sum.

sources.quote: It is the amount that should be invested

higher.tip: Write the rate as a decimal first. That alone earns marks.
For a series of payments, find the present value of each one separately: the first three are $\frac{A}{1+i}$, $\frac{A}{(1+i)^2}$, $\frac{A}{(1+i)^3}$.
Round the final answer as asked. Rounding wrongly, or not at all, loses a mark.

say: You give it the start amount $P$, the final amount $F$, and either the time $t$ or the rate $i$. It finds the one that is missing.
The key idea: in $F = P(1+i)^t$, a **root** frees $i$ and a **log** frees $t$.

how.higher: Higher level uses it as a step inside a loan question: in 2017 Paper 1 Q8(b)(iv), 5 marks, you take logs to find the number of months.
how.ordinary: Ordinary level asks for the rate again and again on Paper 1, taking a root, as a part worth 5 or 10 marks (2016 Q7, 2017 Q1, 2020 Q7, 2023 Q1).

example.question: €20,000 is invested at $4\%$ per annum compound interest. After how many whole years will it first be worth at least €30,000?

steps.title: Isolate the power
steps.say: Divide both sides by $20000$, so that the power of $1.04$ is on its own.

lines.text: If the rate $i$ were missing instead, you would take a **root**: $(1+i)^4 = 1.5$ gives $1+i = 1.5^{1/4}$.

steps.title: Take logs
steps.say: The unknown is in the index. Take $\ln$ of both sides, and $\hl{1}{t}$ comes down as a multiplier.

lines.text: After $10$ years it is not yet $30000$, and after $11$ years it is. Round up.

higher.tip: Once the power is on its own, take logs so that $t$ is no longer an index. That step earns partial credit.
Rearrange the formula carefully before you substitute. Relevant manipulation earns partial credit.
Write the formula with some numbers substituted in. Marks are given for it even if you go no further.

ordinary.tip: Write $F = P(1 + \frac{r}{100})^t$ and substitute whatever you can. Even partial substitution earns marks.
Substitute everything even if you cannot finish. A fully correct substitution earns high partial credit.

say: You give it a regular payment $A$, a rate $i$ for each period and the number of payments $n$. It finds what the savings are worth at the end.
The key idea: each payment grows for a different length of time, so the values form a **geometric series**. One sum formula adds them all.

how.higher: Higher level asks for it on Paper 1 as part of a long question: in 2023 Q8(d), 15 marks, you write the series of payments, use the geometric sum formula, then find the payment $A$.

example.question: Aoife saves €150 at the start of every month for $24$ months. The account pays $0.4\%$ compound interest per month. Find the value of her savings at the end of the $24$ months, to the nearest cent.

steps.title: Write the series
steps.say: The first payment earns interest for $24$ months and the last for $1$ month. Add up the values, starting with the last payment.

steps.title: Read off a, r and n
steps.say: This is a geometric series. Find the first term, the common ratio and the number of terms.

steps.title: Work it out
steps.say: Use the calculator, and round to the nearest cent at the end.

lines.text: If the money went in at the end of each month, the first term would be $150$, not $150(1.004)$. Check which the question says.

higher.tip: Write out the series first. Finding the geometric series is a step of its own and earns marks.
Then substitute $a$, $r$ and $n$ into the geometric sum formula. That is the next marked step.
Include every term, first and last. Leaving out the second or second last term loses a mark.

sources.quote: excludes second and/or second last term

higher.tip: Read whether payments are made at the start or the end of each month. Using the wrong one loses a mark.

sources.quote: Investments made at the end of each month
